questions: How often do you use your phone each day?
What do you mainly use the internet for?
Is there a piece of technology you couldn't live without?
Did you use computers much when you were at school?
Do you think you spend too much time on screens?
tips: Talk about your own habits rather than giving a general speech about technology; Part 1 is personal.
Use frequency expressions naturally: 'every now and then', 'pretty much constantly', 'first thing in the morning'.
A short honest admission ('Probably far too often') followed by a reason sounds more natural than a long list.
usefulPhrases: Pretty much all day, if I'm honest.
It's the first thing I check in the morning.
We only had one computer lab for the whole school.
I've been trying to cut down on...
I try to set limits, but it doesn't always work.

samples.text:
[How often do you use your phone each day?]
I use my phone very often, maybe more than six hours in a day. I use it for chatting with my friend, for social media and also for my work. Sometimes I use it also for watching video before sleeping.

[Is there a piece of technology you couldn't live without?]
I think my phone, because everything is in my phone. My bank account, my map, my photos, everything. If I lost my phone I will be very confused and I cannot do anything.

[Do you think you spend too much time on screens?]
Yes, I think so. Because I work with computer and after that I use my phone, so my eyes are tired. I want to reduce it but it is difficult, because it is already become my habit.
samples.commentary: Fluency & Coherence: answers are relevant and reasonably extended, but rely on 'and also' and 'because' as the main linking devices, and 'phone' is repeated rather than referred to. Lexical Resource: adequate everyday vocabulary with limited precision ('very confused' rather than 'lost' or 'stuck'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy: an attempt at a conditional ('If I lost my phone I will') is inaccurate, and 'it is already become' shows confusion with the present perfect; however, communication is not impeded. Pronunciation: the listing of single nouns ('My bank account, my map, my photos') suggests reasonable chunking, though the overall delivery seems fairly monotonous.

samples.text:
[How often do you use your phone each day?]
Pretty much constantly, if I'm honest. I checked my screen-time report last week and it was averaging about six hours a day, which was a bit of a shock. A lot of that is work messages, though, not just scrolling.

[Is there a piece of technology you couldn't live without?]
My phone, without question. It's basically my wallet, my map and my photo album all in one. If I left it at home, I'd probably turn round and go back for it, even if I was already late.

[Did you use computers much when you were at school?]
Not really. We had one computer lab for the whole school and we only got about an hour a week there, mostly learning how to type and use spreadsheets. It's completely different for kids nowadays.
samples.commentary: Fluency & Coherence: the candidate speaks at length with natural discourse markers ('if I'm honest', 'though', 'Not really') and clear sequencing. Lexical Resource: uses topic vocabulary flexibly and with some idiomatic flair ('screen-time report', 'a bit of a shock', 'all in one'). Grammatical Range & Accuracy: second conditionals and past simple narratives are handled accurately, with complex sentences produced confidently. Pronunciation: the transcript implies effective chunking and some use of contrast ('work messages, though, not just scrolling'), although features such as emphatic stress are only occasionally signalled.

samples.text:
[Is there a piece of technology you couldn't live without?]
I'd love to say no, but realistically it's my phone. It's quietly absorbed so many other objects, my wallet, my camera, even my house keys now that our building uses a digital lock, that losing it would be less an inconvenience than a minor crisis.

[Do you think you spend too much time on screens?]
Undoubtedly. What worries me isn't so much the total hours, because a lot of that is unavoidable for work, but the mindless checking in between. I've started leaving my phone in another room when I read, and it's made a surprising difference to how well I can concentrate.

[Did you use computers much when you were at school?]
Hardly at all. Computer lessons were a once-a-week novelty, and the machines were so slow you'd spend half the lesson waiting for them to start up.
samples.commentary: Fluency & Coherence: answers flow naturally and are developed with nuance, such as distinguishing total hours from 'mindless checking'. Lexical Resource: sophisticated, precise language ('quietly absorbed', 'less an inconvenience than a minor crisis', 'a once-a-week novelty') used with complete naturalness. Grammatical Range & Accuracy: complex structures, including an embedded list inside a result clause and a pseudo-cleft ('What worries me isn't so much...'), are controlled accurately. Pronunciation: the parenthetical insertion and contrastive phrasing imply skilful use of pausing and intonation to guide the listener, with speech that would be easy to follow.
